sources: National Geographic (2013), Dung beetles navigate by the Milky Way (Dacke et al., Current Biology, Lund University and University of Pretoria): first animal known to navigate using the Milky Way; beetles fitted with little cardboard hats that blocked the sky rolled aimlessly; in the Johannesburg Planetarium they oriented as well under the Milky Way alone as under a full starry sky; they must leave the dung pile quickly in a straight line or thieves steal the ball; buried dung balls become food for their young; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/dung-beetles-milky-way-navigation

ScienceDaily (2012), Smolka et al., Dung beetles use their dung ball as a mobile thermal refuge, Current Biology 22(20): balls weigh up to 50 times the beetle's body weight; beetles climb on the moist ball when their front legs and head overheat on hot sand, seven times as often on hot soil; silicone boots on the front legs made them climb less; on the ball they often wipe their faces, which researchers suspect spreads regurgitated liquid to cool them; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/10/121022122054.htm

ScienceDaily (2010), Queen Mary University of London press release on Knell and Simmons, Proceedings of the Royal Society B: the dung beetle Onthophagus taurus can pull 1,141 times its own body weight; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/03/100323212158.htm

beats.say: This beetle steers by the Milky Way, while rolling a ball of poop.
So I shrank myself down to beetle size, to follow one.
The dung beetle. It lives on poop.
It packs dung into a ball, up to fifty times heavier than itself.
Then it rolls it away in a straight line, fast, before another beetle steals it.
At night, it keeps that line, by the glow of the Milky Way.
To test it, scientists put tiny cardboard hats on the beetles, to block the sky.
